memory_verse.label: Bible Reference
memory_verse.text: "Whoever steals an ox or a sheep and slaughters it or sells it must pay back five head of cattle for the ox and four sheep for the sheep." - Exodus 22:1 (NIV)

devotion.label: Devotion
devotion.text:
God's law does not merely say "do not steal." It goes further and asks, "When theft happens, how is it made right?" The thief could not simply return what he took; he had to pay back several times over. Restitution stung, and it was meant to. God wanted wrongdoing to be repaired in a way that both restored the victim and turned the wrongdoer's heart away from doing it again.

There is something deeply healthy in this. Real repentance is not just feeling sorry; it moves toward setting things right where we can. When Zacchaeus met Jesus, he did not stop at an apology — he promised to repay four times over what he had cheated (Luke 19:8). Grace had changed him, and that change showed up in his wallet.

Of course, some debts we can never repay. Our sin against a holy God is beyond our ability to make good. That is why Jesus paid a debt we could not — restoring what we had ruined, at the cost of Himself. When His grace touches us, it stirs in us a desire to make right what we have wronged. Is there something you took, broke, or owe that God is nudging you to repair?

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.text:
Is there a wrong I have done that I need to actively make right?
Do I treat repentance as merely feeling sorry, or as changed action?

prayer.label: Prayer
prayer.text: Father, thank You that Jesus paid the debt I never could. Where I have wronged others, give me the humility to make it right, showing the reality of Your grace in me. Amen.
